citation.title: Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable

standing_assumptions:
The article is P. M. Aronow and A. Carnegie, ‘Beyond LATE: Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect with an Instrumental Variable’, Political Analysis 21 (2013), pp. 492–506. Printed page = PDF page + 491 (printed p. 492 is PDF p. 1). The official supplement (‘Supporting Information Online Appendix A: Simulation Studies’) is paginated A1–A12 and supplement PDF page k is page Ak. The article states no numbered theorem, proposition or lemma; its formal content is the displayed equations (1)–(14), Assumptions 1–3 and the statements in running text and footnotes quoted below. Everything quoted from the article and the supplement was read from the page images (the staged 110 dpi images and 250 dpi renderings of the same PDF pages). Code and package text have no page image and are transcribed from the staged source files; each such passage is marked.
(S1) Setting and potential outcomes. p. 494 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.2: “We now move to the Neyman-Rubin potential outcomes framework, focusing on the case of a binary IV (or treatment assignment) $Z$ and a binary endogenous treatment variable (or treatment received) $D$. Suppose that we have a sample consisting of $n$ units (indexed $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$) independently drawn with equal probability from some large population of interest. For unit $i$, let $Y_{0i}$ be the outcome if untreated, $D_i = 0$, and let $Y_{1i}$ be the outcome if treated, $D_i = 1$. The treatment effect for a given unit $i$ is the difference between unit $i$’s outcomes in both possible states of the world, $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$. Similarly, we may define $D_{0i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to control, $Z_i = 0$, and $D_{1i}$ as the treatment condition of unit $i$ when assigned to treatment, $Z_i = 1$. We will show that the causal estimand recovered by IV estimation will not generally be the ATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$, but will instead be the LATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$.”
(S2) Types. pp. 494–495 (PDF pp. 3–4): “Following Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996), the population may be divided into four groups: always-takers, never-takers, compliers, and defiers. Always-takers are units that receive treatment regardless of whether they are assigned to treatment or control, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 1$. Conversely, never-takers do not receive treatment regardless of their treatment assignment, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 0$. Compliers receive treatment if assigned to treatment and do not receive treatment if assigned to control, so that $D_{0i} = 0$ and $D_{1i} = 1$ (or $D_{1i} > D_{0i}$). Defiers receive treatment if assigned to control and do not receive treatment if assigned to treatment, so that $D_{0i} = 1$ and $D_{1i} = 0$ (or $D_{0i} > D_{1i}$).”
(S3) The five IV assumptions. p. 495 (PDF p. 4): “Using an IV estimator, we may estimate the LATE using five assumptions, as explicated by Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996). First, we assume that the exclusion restriction is valid, or that $Z_i$ only affects $Y_i$ through $D_i$. Second, we assume that $Z_i$ to some degree predicts $D_i$. Third, we invoke the stable unit treatment value assumption, which states that the potential outcomes $D_{0i}$, $D_{1i}$, $Y_{0i}$, and $Y_{1i}$ are fixed and unrelated to the particular arrangement of assignment and treatment statuses. Fourth, we assume that the population contains no defiers, i.e., $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$. Fifth, we assume that $Z_i$ is randomly assigned and thus independent of all potential outcomes.”
(S4) Rendering of (S1)–(S3) used in every target (the article prints no display for it; all validators use it). The observed variables are $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$ and $Y = Y_0 + D(Y_1 - Y_0)$ (exclusion and SUTVA); relevance is $\mathrm{E}(D|Z=1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z=0) \neq 0$; no defiers is $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$; random assignment is: $Z$ is independent of $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$, and of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ where covariates appear (p. 496: “so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$”), with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$. Abbreviations used in the targets and not in the article: $\tau = Y_1 - Y_0$ and $C = \mathbf{1}\{D_1 > D_0\}$.
(S5) SEM framework. p. 493 (PDF p. 2), Section 2.1: “The SEM interpretation of IV estimation posits a linear, additive relationship between an outcome variable ($Y_i$), an endogenous treatment variable ($D_i$), covariates ($Q_{1i}, Q_{2i}....Q_{Ki}$), and an unobserved error term ($u_i$) for each unit $i$, such that $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \lambda_1 Q_{1i} + \lambda_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \lambda_K Q_{Ki} + u_i. \qquad (1)$$” p. 494 (PDF p. 3): “The first equation, or the “first stage,” is a regression of the endogenous variable on the instrument and covariates: $$D_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 Z_i + \delta_1 Q_{1i} + \delta_2 Q_{2i} + .... + \delta_K Q_{Ki} + e_i, \qquad (2)$$ where $e_i$ is a second unobserved error term. [...] Given the model in equations (1) and (2), the SEM IV framework relies on two main assumptions for consistency. First, the correlation between $Z_i$ and $u_i$ must approach zero as $n$ grows. Second, the covariance between $Z_i$ and $D_i$ must converge to a nonzero quantity as $n$ grows. Note, however, that whereas the endogenous variable and covariates in equation (1) are indexed by the subscript $i$, their coefficients (the βs and λs) are not. In other words, the SEM framework assumes constant treatment effects, so that the effect of the treatment is identical for each unit $i$.”
(S6) Compliance score and nested model. p. 496 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.1: “The compliance score is a latent pretreatment covariate that represents the probability of being a complier, conditional on a unit’s pretreatment covariate profile $\mathbf{X}$ (so that $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$). The compliance score for unit $i$, $P_{Ci} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i)$, where $\mathbf{x}_i$ is the covariate vector for unit $i$.” Equations (5) and (6), p. 496: $$P_{A,C,i} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (5)$$ “where $P_{A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is either a complier or an always-taker, $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ is a vector of coefficients to be estimated, and $F(\cdot)$ is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for an arbitrary distribution. For the purposes of this article, we use a probit model, so $F(\cdot) = \Phi(\cdot)$, where $\Phi$ is the Normal CDF. Second, we similarly specify $$P_{A|A,C,i} = \Pr(D_0 = 1|D_1 > D_0 \cup D_0 = 1, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}), \qquad (6)$$ where $P_{A|A,C,i}$ is the conditional probability that unit $i$ is an always-taker conditional on it being either an always-taker or a complier, and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$ are coefficients to be estimated.” Equation (7), p. 497 (PDF p. 6): “[...] our third assumption: $D_i$ is Bernoulli distributed. Then the likelihood for any unit $i$, $$L(P_{A|A,C,i}, P_{A,C,i}|D, Z) = (P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i + P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{D_i}(1 - P_{A,C,i}(1 - P_{A|A,C,i})Z_i - P_{A,C,i}P_{A|A,C,i})^{1-D_i}. \qquad (7)$$ Combining equations (5), (6), and (7), $L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z) = \Pi_{i=1}^{n}((F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i + F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{D_i}(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))Z_i - F(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})F(\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i}))^{1-D_i})$. Thus the ML estimate of $\{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\}$, $$\{\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\} = \underset{\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}},\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}}{\mathrm{argmax}}\left[L(\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}, \theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}|D, Z)\right].$$ After estimating $\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}$ and $\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}$, we may estimate the compliance score for unit $i$, $$\hat{P}_{Ci} = \widehat{\Pr}(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}_i) = F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})(1 - F(\hat\theta_{\mathbf{A|A,C}}\mathbf{x_i})).$$” (On the page this display is followed by a superscript 3, which is the marker of footnote 3 and not an exponent.) The displays between (6) and (7) that carry the misprints of finding P029-E009 are transcribed in P029-T18.
(S7) ICSW estimator. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.3: “In the bivariate case (when there are no covariates), the estimator is simple. Define $\hat{w}_{Ci} = 1/\hat{P}_{Ci}$. The ICSW estimator $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} =$ $$\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iY_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)Y_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iD_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i) - (\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)D_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i))}.$$ An equivalent estimator may be derived using weighted 2SLS (with weights $\hat{w}_{Ci}$). As with the simple 2SLS case, covariates may also be included to reduce sampling variability without any consequence for the asymptotic bias of the estimator.”
(S8) Assumptions 1–3. p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.4: “In order to consistently estimate the ATE using ICSW, three additional assumptions are required. In the appendix, we demonstrate that ICSW is consistent under Assumptions 1–3, along with the IV assumptions and suitable regularity conditions.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “Assumption 1. Latent ignorability of compliance with respect to treatment effect heterogeneity (Frangakis and Rubin 1999; Esterling, Neblo, and Lazer 2011) holds. Assumption 1 entails that, for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$: the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile is equal to the expected value of the treatment effect conditional on a covariate profile and compliance. Put simply, the ATE for all units with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$ is equal to the ATE for compliers with a covariate profile $\mathbf{x}$.” p. 500 (PDF p. 9): “Assumption 2. Consistency of $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ for $P_{Ci}$. Assumption 2 amounts to requiring proper specification of the ML estimator. Application of a flexible parametrization of the covariates in $\mathbf{X}$, as is possible with large samples, will necessarily yield consistency, so long as the rate of growth in the number of estimated parameters is sufficiently slow in $n$. In the case of a saturated model and $F(.)$ as the normal CDF, $\hat{P}_{Ci}$ will be unbiased for the conditional probability of compliance.” p. 500: “Assumption 3. For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$, $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) \in (\epsilon, 1]$, where $\epsilon > 0$. Note that IV estimation already requires the assumption of nonzero compliance in the full population, and we generalize this assumption to every covariate profile.”
(S9) Appendix notation. p. 504 (PDF p. 13): “For clarity, we remove $i$ subscripts to denote all units subject to any conditional probabilities articulated.” p. 499 (PDF p. 8): “where $f(.)$ is the population pdf of $\mathbf{X}$, $g(.)$ is the subpopulation pdf of $\mathbf{X}$ among compliers, and $\Omega = \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$.” The article writes integrals against the density $f$; the validators’ witnesses use covariates with finitely many values, for which $f(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ and the integrals are sums.
(S10) Simulation designs (supplement). Supplement p. A1, ‘Baseline Data Generating Process’ (as printed; the misprints are the subject of P029-T19): $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i \sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1)$; $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h \sim \mathrm{U}(-2, 2)$; $AC_i = \mathbf{I}[2 + a + bX1_i + cX2_i + dX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]$; $A_i = \mathbf{I}[-2 + e + fX1_i + gX2_i + hX3_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 3)]AC_i$; $C_i = AC_i - A_i$; $D_i = D_iZ_i + A_i$; $Y_{0i} = 5AC_i + \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$; $\tau_i = 5 \times (1 + X1_i + X2_i + X3_i)$; $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$. “We observe and use $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$ both as covariates in 2SLS, and for the compliance score model.” Supplement p. A2, under the heading ‘Heterogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as baseline, except: $X1'_i, X2'_i, X3'_i \sim U(-1, 1)$ are the observed covariates, which are entirely independent from $X1_i, X2_i, X3_i$.” Under the heading ‘Homogeneous Treatment Effects, Conditioning on Random Noise’: “Same as the previous DGP, except: $\tau_i = 5, \forall i$.”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equation (3) (the LATE identity under the five IV assumptions, attributed to Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin 1996), the estimator (4) as bivariate 2SLS, and the worked example of Section 3.2
canonical_claim.location: p. 495 (PDF p. 4), equations (3) and (4); pp. 497–498 (PDF pp. 6–7), the gender example
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement, p. 495] “Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996) demonstrate that these five assumptions imply that the “intention-to-treat” effect of $Z_i$ on $Y_i$ (the average effect of treatment assignment on the outcome) divided by the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect of $Z$ on $D$ (the average effect of treatment assignment on treatment received) is equal to the average causal treatment effect for compliers: $$\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = \frac{\mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 0)}{\mathrm{E}(D|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z = 0)}. \qquad (3)$$ The LATE, $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$, can therefore be estimated with $$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{LATE}} = \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_iY_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)Y_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)\right)}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_iD_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)D_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)\right)} \qquad (4)$$ or, equivalently, the bivariate 2SLS estimator.”
[Formal statement of (3), with every hypothesis] Let $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1, Z)$ be random variables with $D_0, D_1, Z \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_0| < \infty$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_1| < \infty$; $D = D_0 + Z(D_1 - D_0)$ and $Y = Y_0 + D(Y_1 - Y_0)$ (exclusion and SUTVA); $\Pr(D_0 > D_1) = 0$ (no defiers); $Z$ independent of $(D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$ (random assignment); and $\mathrm{E}(D|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z = 0) \neq 0$ (relevance). Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}(D|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(D|Z = 0) = \Pr(D_1 > D_0)$; (b) $\mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 1) - \mathrm{E}(Y|Z = 0) = \mathrm{E}[(Y_1 - Y_0)\mathbf{1}\{D_1 > D_0\}] = \Pr(D_1 > D_0)\,\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$; (c) hence (3).
[Equation (4) as bivariate 2SLS] For any real $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ and $D_i, Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ with $0 < \sum_iZ_i < n$ and a nonzero denominator in (4): $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{LATE}} = \dfrac{\sum_i(Z_i - \bar{Z})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_i(Z_i - \bar{Z})(D_i - \bar{D})}$, the instrumental-variables (2SLS) coefficient on $D$ in the regression of $Y$ on an intercept and $D$ with instrument $Z$.
[Worked example, pp. 497–498] “Imagine an experiment where gender is the only determinant of compliance, such that 75% of males comply with their treatment assignments but only 10% of females comply with their treatment assignments. Suppose that the treatment effect for males is 0, but the treatment effect for females is 1. If males and females are represented equally in the population, then the ATE is $\frac{0.5\times0+0.5\times1}{0.5+0.5} = 0.5$. The problem, of course, is that we cannot directly estimate the ATE due to noncompliance. IV estimation recovers the LATE, which we compute using a weighted average, $\frac{0.5\times0.75\times0+0.5\times0.10\times1}{0.5\times0.75+0.5\times0.10} = 0.12$. In this example, the LATE is much lower than the ATE because females are underrepresented among compliers. Recovering the ATE with noncompliance entails weighting units by the inverse of the compliance score, then performing IV estimation. Again computing a weighted average, the estimand recovered by this procedure is the ATE: $\frac{0.5\times0.75\times\frac{1}{0.75}\times0+0.5\times0.10\times\frac{1}{0.10}\times1}{0.5\times0.75\times\frac{1}{0.75}+0.5\times0.10\times\frac{1}{0.10}} = \frac{0.5\times0+0.5\times1}{0.5+0.5} = 0.5$.” Exact content: the first expression equals $1/2$; the second equals $\frac{1/20}{17/40} = \frac{2}{17}$, which rounds to the printed $0.12$ ($0.115 \le 2/17 < 0.125$); the third equals $1/2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Potential outcomes, types and the five IV assumptions: (S1)–(S3); their rendering as hypotheses: (S4). In the example the compliance scores of males and females are $0.75$ and $0.10$ and the three expressions are $\mathrm{E}(\tau)$, $\mathrm{E}(\tau|C = 1) = \sum_xf(x)P_C(x)\mu(x)/\sum_xf(x)P_C(x)$ and $\sum_xf(x)P_C(x)\frac{1}{P_C(x)}\mu(x)/\sum_xf(x)P_C(x)\frac{1}{P_C(x)}$ in the notation of P029-T4, with $f = (1/2, 1/2)$, $P_C = (3/4, 1/10)$, $\mu = (0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P029-H1; an exact population identity, so priority 3. Both readers record that equations (3)–(4) hold under the five listed assumptions and that the sample ratio equals bivariate 2SLS; the example was recomputed by both ($2/17 \approx 0.118$) and again when this list was fixed. The article attributes (3) to Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996) and gives no proof; the derivation (a)–(b) is the standard one, reproduced in the validator's note for P029-E002 (derivation.md, last section). The rest of the headline claim (that the LATE ‘can differ from the ATE’) is witnessed by the example. The sentence comparing the five assumptions with the SEM assumptions on the same page is false (P029-T11, P029-T12) and plays no part in (3). Not part of this target: the statement that (4) is ‘consistent but not unbiased’, and footnote 2 on 2SLS with covariates, which are asymptotic remarks the readers record as holding up.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Consistency of ICSW for the ATE under Assumptions 1–3: Section 3.4 (opening sentences) and the Appendix ‘ICSW Consistency’, equations (8)–(14)
canonical_claim.location: p. 498 (PDF p. 7), Section 3.4, first paragraph; pp. 504–505 (PDF pp. 13–14), Appendix
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement, p. 498] “In order to consistently estimate the ATE using ICSW, three additional assumptions are required. In the appendix, we demonstrate that ICSW is consistent under Assumptions 1–3, along with the IV assumptions and suitable regularity conditions.”
[Appendix, pp. 504–505, as printed] “We derive expressions for the inverse compliance score weighted numerator (average ITT effect) and denominator (average probability of compliance) of equation (3), thus obtaining the asymptotic value of the IV estimator after ICSW. For clarity, we remove $i$ subscripts to denote all units subject to any conditional probabilities articulated. As in equation (3), $\mathrm{ITT} = \Pr(D_1 > D_0)\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0)$, which we may express as a weighted average of the conditional ITTs: $$\mathrm{ITT} = \int_\Omega \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}. \qquad (8)$$ With the equations above, we are now able to apply ICSW, multiplying by the inverse of the compliance score: $\frac{1}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}$. We then divide by the average weight across all units (to normalize the weight). We define the average weight $\overline{w_c} = \int_\Omega \frac{1}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$. We can write the weighted ITT as follows: $$\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \frac{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}. \qquad (9)$$ Since the $\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ terms cancel, equation (9) reduces to $$\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}. \qquad (10)$$ Applying Assumption 1, we can rewrite equation (10) as $\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$. By the law of total probability, the reweighted numerator of the IV estimator is $$\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0). \qquad (11)$$ We can now reweight the denominator of the IV estimator by expanding the definition of the complier population, weighting, and simplifying: $$\Pr(D_1 > D_0) = \int_\Omega \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}, \qquad (12)$$ $$\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \frac{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})}f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}. \qquad (13)$$ Dividing equation (11) by equation (13), we have the asymptotic value of the ICSW estimator, $$\frac{\mathrm{ITT}^w}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w} = \frac{\frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)}{\frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}} = \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0), \qquad (14)$$ which is the ATE. By Slutsky’s theorem, a consistent estimator of $\frac{\mathrm{ITT}^w}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w}$ will be $$\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iY_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)Y_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)\right)}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iD_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\hat{w}}_{Ci}Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)D_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)\right)},$$ as $$\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iY_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)Y_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)\right) \to_p \mathrm{ITT}^w$$ and $$\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_iD_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}Z_i\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)D_i\right)\Big/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{w}_{Ci}(1 - Z_i)\right) \to_p \Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w$$ under suitable regularity conditions.”
[Formal statement] Let the data be independent draws satisfying (S3)–(S4), and let Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold. Then, under suitable regularity conditions, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} \to_p \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$, where $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ is the estimator of Section 3.3 (the display above with a single hat on every weight).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The setting and the five IV assumptions: (S1)–(S4). The compliance score $P_{Ci}$ and its estimate: (S6). $\hat{w}_{Ci} = 1/\hat{P}_{Ci}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$: (S7). Assumptions 1–3: (S8). $f$, $\Omega$: (S9). In the Appendix $\mathrm{ITT}$, $\mathrm{ITT}^w$, $\overline{w_c}$ and $\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w$ are defined by the displays themselves. Equation (9) and the estimator display are transcribed as printed, with the doubled conditioning bar and the doubled hat (finding P029-E009; corrected in P029-T18). The article does not list the ‘suitable regularity conditions’.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact population identities on which the proof rests, for a law satisfying (S3)–(S4) with $P_C(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$ and finite means (integrals against $f$, or sums for a covariate with finitely many values): (L1) equation (8): $\Pr(D_1 > D_0)\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = \int_\Omega P_C(\mathbf{x})\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$, p. 504. (L2) equations (9)–(10), under Assumption 3: $\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$ with $\overline{w_c} = \int_\Omega f(\mathbf{x})/P_C(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$, p. 504. (L3) equation (11), under Assumption 1: $\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$ (law of iterated expectations), p. 504. (L4) equations (12)–(13): $\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w = 1/\overline{w_c}$, p. 504. (L5) equation (14): the ratio is $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0)$, p. 504. (L6) [the link to observable moments, not printed] with $w = 1/P_C(\mathbf{X})$ and $Z$ independent of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$: $\frac{\mathrm{E}(wY|Z = 1)}{\mathrm{E}(w|Z = 1)} - \frac{\mathrm{E}(wY|Z = 0)}{\mathrm{E}(w|Z = 0)} = \frac{\mathrm{E}[wC\tau]}{\mathrm{E}[w]} = \mathrm{ITT}^w$ and $\frac{\mathrm{E}(wD|Z = 1)}{\mathrm{E}(w|Z = 1)} - \frac{\mathrm{E}(wD|Z = 0)}{\mathrm{E}(w|Z = 0)} = \frac{\mathrm{E}[wC]}{\mathrm{E}[w]} = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}$ (P029-T4(i)). (L7) [finite-sample algebra] $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ is the ratio of the difference of the $\hat{w}$-weighted arm means of $Y$ to the difference of the $\hat{w}$-weighted arm means of $D$, and is unchanged when all weights are multiplied by a positive constant.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P029-H2; an asymptotic result, so priority 4. Both readers followed equations (8)–(14) line by line and record that every step is valid under Assumptions 1 and 3 and suitable regularity conditions, after the notation repairs of P029-E009 (the doubled bar in (9), the doubled hat; P029-T18); the step before (11) is the law of iterated expectations, which the article calls the law of total probability. The article gives no list of regularity conditions and does not say in which sense Assumption 2's consistency is meant; one sufficient set, from the validator's corrected argument for P029-E006 (P029-T16(iv)), is: independent identically distributed draws, $Z$ independent of $(\mathbf{X}, D_0, D_1, Y_0, Y_1)$ with $0 < \Pr(Z = 1) < 1$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_0| < \infty$, $\mathrm{E}|Y_1| < \infty$, and $\max_{i \le n}|\hat{P}_{Ci} - P_{Ci}| \to_p 0$. These are this audit's, not the article's, and a formalization that proves the limit should state them as its own hypotheses. The exact content is (L1)–(L7). Findings that touch the surrounding text and not the result: P029-E003 and P029-E004 (comparisons and a sufficiency remark about Assumption 1), P029-E006 (the reason given for ignoring Winsorization). The Winsorized estimator actually used in the applications is covered by P029-T16.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The limit of ICSW when Assumption 1 fails (complier effects reweighted to the population covariate distribution), the LATE as an integral against the complier covariate density, and 2SLS as the special case with no covariates
canonical_claim.location: p. 499 (PDF p. 8), paragraph beginning ‘But what if treatment effects are heterogeneous’ and the two displays; pp. 499–500 (PDF pp. 8–9), the following paragraph; Appendix equations (10) and (13), p. 504 (PDF p. 13)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement, p. 499] “But what if treatment effects are heterogeneous and we have failed to identify the sufficient conditioning set? As Assumption 1 no longer holds, the ICSW estimator is now biased, even asymptotically. However, ICSW will still recover an internally valid causal effect, not on the full population of interest, but for some population that has a covariate profile that matches that of the full population. To see this, we can compare two expressions. Through simple manipulation of expectations, the LATE may be written as $$\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\frac{\Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}}{\Pr(D_1 > D_0)} = \int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})g(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x},$$ where $f(.)$ is the population pdf of $\mathbf{X}$, $g(.)$ is the subpopulation pdf of $\mathbf{X}$ among compliers, and $\Omega = \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{X})$. Manipulating equations (10) and (13) from the appendix, the asymptotic value of the ICSW estimator under failure of Assumption 1 will be $$\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}.$$ The difference between $g(.)$ and $f(.)$ characterizes the nature of the adjustment performed by ICSW.” pp. 499–500: “When the ATE is the parameter of interest, the limiting value of the ICSW estimator is thus typically more sensible than that of 2SLS/IV, as ICSW incorporates available covariate information. In fact, 2SLS represents the special case of ICSW where no covariates are included in the compliance score estimation process.”
[Formal statement] Let the data be independent draws satisfying (S3)–(S4), with Assumptions 2 and 3 and without Assumption 1. Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0) = \int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})g(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$ with $g(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})/\Pr(D_1 > D_0)$, the density of $\mathbf{X}$ among compliers; (b) under suitable regularity conditions $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} \to_p \int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$; (c) if the estimated compliance scores are the same positive number for every unit (no covariates in the compliance-score model), then $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{LATE}}$ of equation (4) for every sample in which both are defined.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The setting: (S1)–(S4). The compliance score: (S6). $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$: (S7). Assumptions 1–3: (S8). $f$, $g$, $\Omega$: (S9) and the quoted passage. Equations (10) and (13): transcribed in P029-T26. Equation (4): P029-T25.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact statements on which the result rests: (L1) [Bayes] $g(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})/\Pr(D_1 > D_0)$ and $\Pr(D_1 > D_0) = \int_\Omega \Pr(D_1 > D_0|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$ (equation (12)), which give (a), p. 499. (L2) Appendix equations (10) and (13), which do not use Assumption 1: $\mathrm{ITT}^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}\int_\Omega \mathrm{E}(Y_1 - Y_0|D_1 > D_0, \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$ and $\Pr(D_1 > D_0)^w = \frac{1}{\overline{w_c}}$, p. 504; their ratio is the limit in (b). (L3) the link to observable weighted moments, P029-T26 (L6), equivalently P029-T4(i) and (iii). (L4) [finite-sample, exact] if $\hat{w}_{Ci} = k > 0$ for all $i$, the constant cancels from each of the four weighted means and the Section 3.3 estimator equals (4); this is (c).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P029-H4; an asymptotic result, so priority 4. Both readers obtained the limit by dividing (10) by (13) and checked the LATE integral by Bayes' rule; it holds given Assumptions 2 and 3 (with the same unlisted regularity conditions as P029-T26). The sentence that precedes this passage on p. 499 (independence of effects and compliance) is the subject of P029-E004 and is false (P029-T3); witness (A) there is an instance of (b): $f(0)\mu(0) + f(1)\mu(1) = 7/16$, with LATE $= 1/2$. The exact difference between the two limits, $\mathrm{LATE} - \operatorname{plim}\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \mathrm{Cov}(P_C(\mathbf{X}), \mathrm{E}[\tau|C, \mathbf{X}])/\Pr(D_1 > D_0)$, is the raising reader's and is P029-T4(iv); it is not in the article. Not part of the target: the evaluative remarks (‘internally valid’, ‘typically more sensible’), which are interpretation; and the behaviour under a misspecified compliance-score model (one reader notes that the limit is then $\mathrm{E}[P_C\mu/q]/\mathrm{E}[P_C/q]$ for the limiting score $q$, still a weighted average of complier effects but not matched to the population covariate distribution).
